The story makes sophisticated use of metaphor, particularly through its central, extended metaphor of the geological "benchmark." Hollis, a retired surveyor, explains how brass disks cemented into bedrock slowly move along with the continent over time until "it just isn't where it says it is anymore." He later explicitly connects this to his own life and his estrangement from his daughter ("We drifted, like the benchmarks. You look up one day and the numbers don't match"). This metaphor also resonates with the broader theme of death and loss in the story—such as his ex-wife dying eight months before he found out, or the deceased woman in the car whose loved ones are still "living in the world where [she's] alive," operating on outdated information before reality catches up to the "numbers." 

Additionally, the author uses smaller, evocative metaphors and figurative comparisons throughout the prose to establish a poignant, quiet tone, such as describing the dead woman's cool skin as "the temperature of a room no one has been in all day," and the road at the end "unspooling in the headlights."
